To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

perceived routine burden was significantly correlated with child anxiety and asthma QOL; perceived routine burden significantly predicted both child anxiety and QQL; perceived routine burden predicted child anxiety through its effect on rejection/criticism; perceived routine burden did not predict child asthma QOL through its effects on rejection/critism; perceived routine burden also predicted child anxiety through mother intrusiveness; and perceived routine burden did predict child asthma QL through mother intrusivenes.
perceived burden of routine care was associated with child anxiety and QQL through its influence on mother-child interaction patterns.
perceived burden of routine care for children with asthma significantly predicted children's mental health and asthma-related QOL through its influence on mother-child rejection and criticism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the family in the management of chronic illness in children.
how families with a child who has asthma manage the child's asthma and how these family processes are related to child adjustment.
understanding the impact of family climate on child mental health in the context of asthma management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
perceived burden of routine care is associated with mother-child rejection/criticisms, which in turn are related to poorer child well-being.
the family climate of routine asthma management affects the well-being of children with asthma, and that this effect occurs via the family's interactional patterns.
the family climate of routine asthma management is an important factor to consider in the treatment of pediatric asthma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the family climate of routine asthma management is a key determinant of child well-being, particularly when perceived as burdensome by mothers.

the more burden a mother perceives in managing her child’s asthma, the less likely she is to be able to regulate the routine asthma care and the more likely she is to reject/criticize her child, which in turn, is related to poorer child adjustment to the illness.
family climate is important to the adjustment of children with chronic physical conditions, and that family-based interventions may have an important role in promoting child well-being.
The main takeaway from our work is that
family climate is important in determining how well a child is able to cope with asthma.
families with a child who has asthma can be supported in ways that help them manage the child's asthma and improve the child's mental health.
the family climate of routine asthma management can have a significant influence on child mental health and well-being.
